text: Richard Huemer (January 2, 1898 – November 30, 1979) was an American animator active during the Golden Age of Animation. While working as an artist-illustrator in the Bronx, New York City, he began his animation career at the Raoul Barré cartoon studio in 1916. In 1923, he joined the Fleischer Studio, where he developed the Koko the Clown character, redesigned the clown for more efficient animation, and reduced the studio’s reliance on the Rotoscope for smooth motion. He created Ko-Ko's canine companion, Fitz, and established the drawing style that defined the series. After moving to Hollywood, Huemer worked as an animator and director at the Charles Mintz studio, where he developed the character Scrappy. He later joined the Disney Studio, remaining there from April 16, 1933, to February 28, 1973, with a three-year break from 1948 to 1951 during which he pioneered animated TV commercials and co-created with Paul Murry the comic strip The Adventures of Buck O'Rue. Huemer collaborated extensively with Joe Grant on several projects, including Fantasia (as story director), Dumbo (as screenplay), and various propaganda films supporting the U.S. war effort in World War II. Notably, Huemer and Grant submitted Dumbo to Walt Disney not as a completed storyboard, but as a series of storyboard "chapters" ending in cliffhangers, a strategy that successfully generated Disney’s interest in the project. In February 1973, Huemer was presented with a Mousecar by the Disney Studio during a ceremony attended by fellow animators. He received the Winsor McCay Award at the Annie Awards in October 1978, introduced by Ward Kimball. On October 10, 2007, Huemer's son, Dr. Richard P. Huemer, accepted the Disney Legends award in his father's name.
